newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile sees 1997 mackerel catches tumbling.
newsitem.headline: Chile sees 1997 mackerel catches tumbling.

text.p: Chile expects mackerel catches to fall 25 percent to three million tonnes this year as the result of fishing bans which have kept fleets in port for three months this year, said a top government official Friday.

"Catches will fall to three million tonnes, or even less, as the result of low catches in the first few months of the year which cannot be made in the second half of 1997," Fishing Undersecretary Juan Manuel Cruz told a news conference.

In a move unprecedented in Chile's fishing industry, the government has imposed five temporary bans this year on catching mackerel -- the main ingredient for fishmeal -- to protect shoals of young fish close to northern shores.
"There has never been a ban on mackerel fishing in Chile before. This year fleets have been halted for 90 days," he said.
The young fish have been drawn into the coastal fishing grounds by higher-than-usual ocean temperatures caused by the El Nino phenomenon in the southern Pacific Ocean, he said.
The government lifted the latest ban Friday after studies showed shoals of larger fish within Chile's coastal waters, reducing the risk of fleets catching smaller, immature fish.
Companies will be able to fish for mackerel until August when the fishing season is suspended as usual until January.
Chile is the world's second largest fishmeal producer with its fleets catching 3.9 million tonnes of mackerel last year.
The slump in mackerel catches this year will reduce fishmeal production by some 200,000 tonnes to around 800,000 tonnes, said Cruz.
Some of the shortfall will be made up by a rise in anchovy catches with fish moving into Chile's northern waters from cooler Peruvian coasts as a result of El Nino, said Cruz.
Anchovy catches in north Chile are expected to rise 50 percent on 1996, he said.
